10126-home-life-of-the-lancashire-factor:
Edwin Waugh wrote this first-hand account of Lancashire mill workers during the Cotton Famine of the 1860s, when the American Civil War cut off raw cotton. He visited Blackburn, Preston, Wigan, and other mill towns to see how families lived without wages. Letters and speeches on relief close the book.

Waugh describes bare cupboards, idle mills, charity, and the pride of people who kept going with little help. Wandering minstrels and wayside scenes show both humor and grief in hard times. Readers get a humane, ground-level record of working-class endurance during a famous industrial crisis.
10638-the-youthful-wanderer-an-account-o:
Geo. H. Heffner published The Youthful Wanderer in 1876 as a guide for young Americans seeing Europe for the first time. His tour runs through England, France, Belgium, Holland, Germany and the Rhine, Switzerland, Italy, and Egypt. Steamships had lately made such a trip faster and cheaper, and Heffner argues that travel should finish a young person's schooling.

The book mixes plain travel notes with advice on what to see and how to learn from it, from old cities to the Nile. Its tone is earnest and instructive, aimed at readers taking their first glimpses of the Old World. Modern readers get a friendly record of how Americans toured Europe in the 1870s, before mass tourism.
11449-an-enquiry-into-the-obligations-of:
William Carey's 1792 Enquiry into the Obligations of Christians to Use Means for the Conversion of the Heathens launched the modern missionary movement with a question from Paul. how shall they hear without a preacher, and how shall they preach except they be sent. Carey surveys the religious state of nations, the success of former undertakings, and the practicability of further ones, answering the objection that home ignorance should supersede foreign missions.

Carey grants thousands at home are far from God, but argues home hearers have Bibles, ministers. Means of grace, while many abroad have no Bible, no written language, no ministers, and no good government. The pamphlet's logic founded the Baptist Missionary Society. For church historians, it is the founding text of Protestant world missions.
12828-two-ghostly-mysteries-a-chapter-in:
J. Sheridan Le Fanu's Two Ghostly Mysteries pairs A Chapter in the History of a Tyrone Family, first published in 1836, with The Murdered Cousin of 1851. The Tyrone tale comes as an extract from the legacy of Francis Purcell, priest of Drumcoolagh, retold as nearly as possible in the narrator's own words. A woman who lived the strange scenes tells them herself.

Ghostly dread builds through a voice whispering of blood upon a lady's throat, sending her to the door in horror to find no speaker. Le Fanu's gothic craft lies in that slow, personal terror. The pair suits readers who like classic Irish ghost stories told with restraint.
13298-the-california-birthday-book-prose:
George Wharton James's 1909 California Birthday Book, from the Arroyo Guild Press of Los Angeles, gathers prose and poetical selections from living California authors, each with a brief biographical sketch. James dedicates the book to his wife, his literary partner, whose judgment aided the selections. The introduction hails California as land of golden thoughts, golden hills, golden mines, and golden deeds.

One poem, on San Francisco after the fire, sees splendor crumble into dust in a day. Yet three short years mark a sure rebirth to splendid urban might, refined in flame like iron into steel. Later, a September entry sings meadow larks across the fields, sweet, sweet, sweet, and calls life love. The book is a charming anthology of California writing.
13360-missionary-survey-as-an-aid-to-int:
Roland Allen and Thomas Cochrane's 1920 Missionary Survey as an Aid to Intelligent Co-operation in Foreign Missions argues that missions must be studied as one work, not three. Allen, sometime S.P.G. missionary in North China, and Cochrane, late principal of Union Medical College, Peking, wrote the book together after studying the material and settling what to include. The survey is methodical and practical.

Its tables count total population, Christian constituency, and non-Christian constituency by district, marking places occupied where resident Christians live, few or many. A later chapter unifies evangelistic, medical, and educational work, holding that a mission ought not to be three separate things but one, since its impression on non-Christians comes from the combination. The book shaped mission planning in its day.
13635-new-york-times-current-history-the:
The New York Times Current History volume for the European War, covering the beginning of the war to March 1915, gathers essays, letters, and documents from the first months of the conflict. George Bernard Shaw's Common Sense About the War leads, answered in turn by Arnold Bennett, Cunninghame Graham, Christabel Pankhurst, and others.

Shaw argues, in a letter to the Daily News, that Bennett's case for Germany is strong and deserves a fair hearing, while his critics accuse him of empty cleverness. Later sections follow the fighting in Southwest Africa and the wider war. The volume is a primary record of how writers argued about the war while it was still new, before the long grind set in.
14136-the-outdoor-girls-at-the-hostess-h:
Laura Lee Hope's wartime girls' book sends the Outdoor Girls to a hostess house, doing their best for soldiers. Grace, Amy, Betty, and Mollie dress for afternoons, tease each other about boys following like Mary's little lamb, and plan to watch a bayonet drill Sergeant Mullins invited them to see. Town girls, the friends chuckle, cannot steal soldiers' hearts away.

Parting gives the story its ache. Betty whispers dear to Allen as he leaves, and he answers that whatever he does over there will be because of her. A whistle shrieks, hands tighten, and the train moves amid cheering. Hope, author of the Bobbsey Twins and Moving Picture Girls, writes clean, cheerful adventure with a wartime edge. Service, friendship, and first love share the volume, and the hostess house stands for home comfort carried near the front.
14170-the-nursery-volume-17-no-100-april:
April 1875 brought the hundredth number of The Nursery, a Boston monthly magazine for youngest readers. Uncle Charles leads with nature lessons in dialogue form, as Arthur asks Uncle Oscar about pictures in a book. Barley yields pearl barley when stripped, rounded, and polished in a mill, Oscar explains. Rye follows, a grain grass that thrives in cold weather and poor, light soils.

A stolen bird's nest supplies the moral tale. Two sparrows build by a wayside tree, hatch four young in May, and starve themselves to feed hungry mouths stretching for food. Sugar lessons close the run, noting northern cane sugar cannot match cane sugar in cheapness. Simple words, pictures, and kindness to birds mark a magazine made for small children learning to read the world.
14232-a-celtic-psaltery-being-mainly-ren:
Alfred Perceval Graves published A Celtic Psaltery in 1917, rendering Irish and Welsh poetry into English verse. Dedicated to David Lloyd George, prime minister, the book recalls an Eisteddfod floor flooded with choral song and a prince kneeling in fealty at investiture. Graves calls Lloyd George a Celtic seer who scaled the peak and saw freedom breaking into birth above hatred and division.

Poems range from sacred to playful. A church bell in the night wins a tryst over any light-minded maiden, while a crucifixion lyric pairs Christ's wan face with a far-flown winter swan. A pilgrim learns Rome offers small gain if the King sought there travels not from Erin. Dead Lon of Kilgarrow draws a lament for schools and scholars. Shepherds, woodmen, maidens, and fishers throng a mount to find Christ healing deaf, blind, and lame. Verse translation here serves devotion and nation together.
15856-sutherland-and-caithness-in-saga-t:
A history of Scotland's far north in saga time by James Gray, issued by Oliver and Boyd in Edinburgh in 1922, printed at Stromness. Gray first gave the work as a presidential address to the Viking Society for Northern Research, then enlarged it. His aim is to interest Sutherland and Caithness folk in their own early history. Three sagas bear on it, where Scottish records almost wholly fail.

Jarls and Freskyns, Orkney and Shetland, and the Norse settlement fill the pages. Gray weighs saga evidence against place names and scant records. The tone stays scholarly yet local, proud of the north. The book still serves readers of Viking Scotland: a careful bridge between saga tale and county history.
16822-memorial-addresses-on-the-life-and:
Congress issued this 1892 book of memorial addresses on William H. F. Lee, a representative from Virginia, spoken in the House and Senate in the Fifty-second Congress, first session. The Government Printing Office printed it by order of Congress, with eight thousand copies struck, including fifty bound in full morocco for his family and a portrait to go with the text.

Speakers praise Lee's life and character in formal eulogy, as Congress did for its dead members. The volume shows the rituals of public grief in 1892: praise, record, and print for kin and state. Readers of political history will find a short, formal portrait of a Virginia congressman, useful for its tone more than for deep biography.
17475-the-lobster-fishery-of-maine-bulle:
John N. Cobb, agent of the United States Fish Commission, wrote this study of the lobster fishery of Maine for the commission's bulletin, volume nineteen, pages 241 to 265. The e-text was prepared while its editor served as Penobscot Bay watch in Rockland, Maine. Tables and pictures accompany the study in its fuller form.

Readers learn how Maine lobsters were caught, handled, and sold, and how the fishery was managed at the turn of the century. Cobb writes as a government scientist, with figures and plain description. The bulletin suits readers of fisheries history and of Maine's working coast.
17512-prairie-farmer-vol-56-no-1-january:
Prairie Farmer, a weekly journal for the farm, orchard, and fireside, issued this number in Chicago on Saturday, January 5, 1884, as volume fifty-six, number one. The paper had been established in 1841 and cost two dollars a year in advance. Its contents page, moved to the front for ease of use, opens with agriculture, including a piece on tall meadow oat grass.

As a single weekly issue, the paper mixes farming advice, orchard notes, and household reading for prairie families. Some pages of the scanned copy had torn corners, and missing text is marked in the transcription. Readers get a direct look at Midwestern farm life in the 1880s, through the paper that served it week by week.
17781-the-golden-censer-or-the-duties-of:
John McGovern wrote this book on the duties of today and the hopes of the future, called The Golden Censer. He was of the Chicago Tribune and author of a history of communism and other works. It was sold by subscription only through the Union Publishing House, with offices in Chicago, Columbus, Kansas City, Minneapolis, San Francisco, Lexington, and Buffalo. Copyright dates run 1881 to 1882, with publication in 1884.

McGovern's preface takes pleasure in laying his work before readers, in the manner of a popular moral and devotional writer. Readers get a late Victorian book of duty and hope, earnest and improving. The volume suits readers of subscription literature and of American moral writing.
18549-the-von-toodleburgs-or-the-history:
F. Colburn Adams wrote this comic family history, published in Philadelphia by Claxton, Remsen and Haffelfinger in 1868, with drawings by A. R. Waud. It follows the Von Toodleburgs, a family that calls itself very distinguished, from their ancient heads to their later fortunes.

The story opens near Nyack on the Hudson in 1803. Honest farmer Hanz Toodleburg lives with his neighbors, who call him Toodlebug. They elect him hog-reeve each year, an honor he always declines. Book one carries the family through town indignation, a night expedition, and a voyage round Cape Horn, in a spirit of broad American humor.
19953-origin-and-development-of-form-and:
William H. Holmes traced the origin and development of form and ornament in ceramic art. Living tribes' art, he argues, can illuminate pre-Columbian art's obscure passages. Peoples least influenced by whites preserve the oldest methods best. Holmes supplements excavation with ethnology throughout the study. Potsherds become evidence of whole design systems here. The work appeared under the Bureau of Ethnology's imprint.

Holmes was a geologist, artist, and archaeologist in one career. His ceramic studies classified decoration by its growth from technique. Basket marks, coils, and tools explain painted designs in his theory. The argument shaped American archaeology for decades. His drawings alone make the volume valuable. It is a founding text of ceramic anthropology.
20301-a-museum-for-young-gentlemen-and-l:
A Museum for Young Gentlemen and Ladies is a private tutor for youth at home. It gathers facts on many subjects in one small, handy book. The original was tiny, about nine centimeters in size and scope. Each line held only eight or nine words on average there.

That small scale shaped the plain, packed style of the whole work. Such books taught manners, nature, trade, and morals before school was common. A museum, then, meant a storehouse of wonders, not a building alone. Young readers got a pocket tutor full of facts worth knowing.
20434-the-boy-scouts-first-camp-fire-or-:
The Boy Scouts' First Camp Fire, published in 1913, follows a troop of boys learning scouting with the Silver Fox patrol. Camp life, hikes, and tests of skill fill the chapters. The boys learn to watch, listen, and remember what they see.

One lesson comes straight from the instruction book. A true scout keeps his eyes and ears open to see and hear everything. The more a boy can recall from a store window after one minute's look, the higher he stands. Such drills, mixed with outdoor fun, made these books favorites with the first scouting generation.
21047-the-nursery-no-109-january-1876-vo:
Fine drawings in this number need no praise from us, The Nursery tells its readers for January 1876. Merrill's Christmas at the North and Sheppard's at the South earn warm words. Harrison Weir's two dogs are called capital work in the same breath.

The Nursery, a monthly magazine for the youngest readers, mixes tales, verse, and plates. Large print and short pieces suit children just past picture books alone. Volume nineteen's New Year number shows its cosy store at full charm. Such magazines taught generations of American children to love the printed page, one short, bright piece at a time.
22028-the-war-service-of-the-1-4-royal-b:
C. R. M. F. Cruttwell, a former captain in the battalion, wrote The War Service of the 1/4 Royal Berkshire Regiment at his old commanding officer's request. The history first ran in the Berkshire Chronicle in 1920, while the Great War was still fresh. Berkshire families then paid to see it reprinted as a book. Cruttwell follows a Territorial battalion of county men through the whole war.

Such regimental histories record marches, trenches, attacks, and the names of the fallen. This one was made for the men who served and the homes that lost them. Its value now lies in the detail only an insider could supply. It shows how one English county battalion endured the First World War.
22627-german-science-reader-an-introduct:
Charles F. Kroeh wrote the German Science Reader, a 1907 textbook introducing students of physics, chemistry, and engineering to scientific German. In Kroeh's day, German was a working language of science, and no researcher could thrive without reading it. His reader bridges language study and the laboratory.

His method is practical: translate a passage, then read the German again and again, aloud, with pauses and emphasis, as if telling the thoughts to another person. Pronouncing words and sentences, he argues, fixes them in memory. Graded readings in the sciences follow the advice. The book now serves language historians and any scientist who still meets older German literature in the stacks.
23107-a-book-of-discovery-the-history-of:
M. B. Synge marches through exploration history in A Book of Discovery. Her contents run like a drum roll. The Vikings sail the northern seas. The end of medieval exploration comes. Prince Henry of Portugal appears. Bartholomew Diaz reaches the stormy cape. Vasco da Gama reaches India. Balboa sees the Pacific. Magellan sails round the world. Cortes explores and conquers Mexico.

Synge wrote history for young readers with a storyteller's pace, and this survey covers the whole age of sail and discovery. Each chapter turns a voyage into a tale while keeping the map in view. The viewpoint is British and of its time, proud of the road from Diaz to the empire. As an introduction that generations actually finished, the book earned its long life.
23576-quadrupeds-what-they-are-and-where:
Captain Mayne Reid wrote this book of quadrupeds, what they are and where found, for young readers keen on four footed beasts. Twenty four chapters take up a kind at a time, with dogs, domestic and wild, earning two chapters each, and some twenty fine pictures showing many beasts of each group.

Reid aims to inform competently, not to dazzle, and his preface states the plan plainly. Girls as well as boys, the book's modern editor notes, will enjoy it as much as Reid's intended boy readers. The phrase well known recurs more than forty times, perhaps too freely for beginners. Young naturalists will gain a solid, picture rich start in zoology, from farm beasts to wild kinds across the globe.
23665-the-peacock-at-home-and-the-butter:
Three popular animal verses share this London volume, printed by Grant and Griffith in its twenty-third edition. The Peacock at Home, by a Lady, answers an earlier insect poem. Stung that butterflies and bees hold balls while birds and beasts stay home, the peacock vows to give a fête of his own. He sends carrier pigeons out with cards for Saint Valentine's Day.

Beside it stand Mr. Roscoe's Butterfly's Ball, the poem that started the fashion, and The Fancy Fair, or Grand Gala at the Zoological Gardens. Together they form a charming set of Regency-era verses in which beasts, birds, and insects ape human society, parties, and pride.
23857-the-new-york-and-albany-post-road-:
C. G. Hine published The New York and Albany Post Road in 1906, an account of a jaunt on foot made at sundry convenient times between May and November 1905. His road runs from Kings Bridge to the ferry at Crawlier, over against Albany, a hundred and fifty miles through the Hudson Valley.

Hine calls the valley, above all other places in this country, a blend of historic and romantic interest with natural beauty. Its dust was stirred by the Indian's moccasin and the soldier's boot, its echoes are the stage driver's whip and the startled deer's whistle. Hills named for wild boar and wild cat line a road that was once the artery of travel and trade.
2396-history-of-the-catholic-church-from:
James MacCaffrey's History of the Catholic Church carries the story from the Renaissance through the Reformation and into the modern age. The volume covers councils, reformers, missions, and the Church's relations with states, written from a Catholic scholar's viewpoint with clarity and detail. MacCaffrey aims at fairness within his tradition.

The book serves students of church history as a solid, readable survey. Its early twentieth century perspective shows in its judgments. Readers seeking a Catholic account of these centuries will find a thorough guide. MacCaffrey taught church history at Maynooth, Ireland's national seminary.
24409-our-common-insects-a-popular-accou:
A. S. Packard, Junior, author of A Guide to the Study of Insects, wrote this popular account of the insects of fields, forests, gardens, and houses, with four plates and 268 woodcuts. It was published at Salem by the Naturalists' Agency, with Boston and New York publishers, in 1873, and entered in 1878. Packard dedicates the little volume to Samuel H. Scudder, drawn to him years before by a shared love of insects and their ways.

The book mainly reprints essays from the American Naturalist, volumes one through five, 1867 to 1871, hoping readers gain a closer acquaintance with the habits and forms of common insects. Its introduction was written expressly for the book, as was chapter thirteen, Hints on the Ancestry of Insects, where classification is tested by the theory of evolution. Readers get common insects, closely watched.
2455-history-of-the-catholic-church-from:
This volume of James MacCaffrey's History of the Catholic Church continues the story from the Renaissance through the Reformation era, covering the Church's trials, councils, and missions. MacCaffrey surveys the religious wars, the Council of Trent, and the rise of new orders, with a scholar's detail and a Catholic's sympathy. The narrative is clear and orderly.

The book complements its companion volumes for a full survey of the period. Its judgments reflect early twentieth century Catholic historiography. Church history students will find a reliable reference. The volume covers the Council of Trent in particular detail.
2634-the-evolution-of-theology-an-anthro:
Thomas Henry Huxley treats theology as a human phenomenon in this eighth essay from Science and Hebrew Tradition, subtitled an anthropological study. He traces the origin, growth, decline, and fall of beliefs about beings like men but without bodies, powers, and dispositions.

Such speculations, Huxley argues, can be studied like any other part of human culture, with causes and stages. The essay is bold, systematic, and free of mockery, even as it denies theology a special exemption from inquiry. Readers get a pioneering attempt to put religion itself under the lens of science.
28139-the-nursery-november-1877-vol-xxii:
The Nursery for November 1877, volume twenty-two, number five, is a Boston monthly for youngest readers from John L. Shorey. Verse opens with Steering for Home, a sailor's song of wind, spray, and a ship bound for port, and goes on to naughty pigs, a butterfly and grasshopper, and a mosquito. Prose covers Sarah's picture, Kitty Bell, a clever fox, and Ponto's dinner.

Further tales treat a pet pigeon, a farm, ironing lessons, and boys with rabbits, with an eighth astronomy lesson and a drawing lesson. An apple-tree song with music closes the number. The issue keeps the magazine's usual blend of animals, work, and gentle morals.
28140-the-nursery-december-1877-vol-xxii:
The Nursery for December 1877, volume twenty-two, number six, closes the year with Christmas tales for youngest readers. Prose covers starlings and sparrows, Katie and Waif, Amy and Robert in China, two old horses, and a robin friend, with drawing lessons and notes on horse sense. Verse repeats Steering for Home and adds a fox and crow, swallows and robins, and Christmas, set to music.

A comic verse play, The Last Guest, has Mary scold Tommy for eating a pheasant meant for breakfast. The issue, published in Boston by John L. Shorey, blends holiday cheer with animals and manners. It shows the magazine ending its year as it began: kind, simple, and full of pictures.
30586-the-exploits-of-juve-being-the-sec:
The Exploits of Juve, second in the Fantomas detective series, carries a tangled authorship note. The cover names Pierre Souvestre and Marcel Allain as authors, while the title page lists Emile Souvestre and Marcel Allain. Pierre Souvestre lived 1874 to 1914 and Marcel Allain 1885 to 1969, while Emile Souvestre, great-uncle of Pierre, lived 1806 to 1854 and died before Allain was born.

The note resolves the confusion in favor of Pierre Souvestre as Allain's partner. Juve, the detective who hunts Fantomas, drives the exploits in this second volume, with crime, pursuit, and disguise at its heart. The book offers classic French detective thrills for readers of the Fantomas saga.
31065-try-again-or-the-trials-and-triump:
Oliver Optic's story for young folks follows Harry West, a boy who quarrels with Squire Walker, quits the poorhouse to work the river. Chapter by chapter he faces hard navigation, defeat, tight places, a big snake, and new friends. He reaches the city, grows suddenly rich, works as a stable boy, and at last goes into the drygoods business and revisits Rockville.

The book's moral is in its title: every setback is a reason to try again, and Harry learns that a defeat can sometimes teach more than a victory. Written in Optic's brisk, earnest style for boy readers, it offers adventure, honest work, and good deeds as the road from a poor start to a respectable life.
32420-a-yankee-flier-with-the-r-a-f:
Al Avery's boys' novel, copyrighted in 1941, follows Stan Wilson, a Yankee flier serving with the Royal Air Force. The story opens in a mess room blaring swing music. Stan enters with blue eyes, a half-smile, and a zest for living born of Colorado canyons and the limitless spaces a flier sees. Seldom does danger stop Stan from laughing at himself.

Chapters follow a glory trail, cloud tag, Bill O'Malley, new quarters, and O'Malley bagging a Jerry gun. Sea dogs, salt spray, Stan's past, a special mission, ground sleuthing, and Luftwaffe in reverse carry the action. Avery mixes air combat, humour, and comradeship, giving young readers a wartime adventure about an American volunteer flying with Britain.
33364-a-new-subspecies-of-the-fruit-eati:
J. Knox Jones and Gary L. Phillips's paper describes a new subspecies of the fruit-eating bat Sturnira ludovici, from western Mexico. Published in March 1964 as volume fourteen, number sixteen of the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History publications, the paper runs from pages 475 to 481, with one figure. Its authors set out how the new form differs from its kin.

The paper suits readers of mammalogy and taxonomy, offering a short, technical case for a new name. Its tone is precise and measured, with measurements and comparisons to back its claim. For bat researchers, it is a useful, if narrow, source, adding one more form to the rich bat fauna of Mexico.
4521-narrative-of-the-overland-expeditio:
Frederick J. Byerley compiled this account from the journals of brothers Frank and Alexander Jardine, who drove an overland party from Rockhampton toward Cape York in northern Queensland. Published at Brisbane in 1867, the narrative records the push to open and settle the far north of Australia. It names stations, rivers, and camps as the party moves through country that few Europeans had crossed.

Readers follow the daily work of travel: finding water, managing stock, meeting Aboriginal people, and coping with heat, floods, and short supplies. The book also sets the trip beside the wider settlement of Cape York under their father. It suits readers who want a first-hand colonial expedition story, told in plain journal style rather than polished history.
499-tom-swift-in-the-land-of-wonders-or-:
Victor Appleton, a house pen name, sends boy inventor Tom Swift to Honduras in this series tale, number twenty in the set. Professor Bumper seeks a lost idol of gold, and Tom, Ned, and friends follow maps, jungles, and vampire bats to a hidden cavern. A rival, poisoned arrows, and a revolving stone bar the way.

Appleton writes brisk, gadget-filled adventure for young readers, with Tom's machines solving each snag. The idol quest ends in a storm and a narrow escape. The book captures the Tom Swift formula at full tilt: pluck, science, and a treasure just beyond the next trap.
7497-further-adventures-of-quincy-adams-:
Charles Felton Pidgin's first Quincy Adams Sawyer had been heralded as the work of an unknown author. Published eight years earlier, it won hundreds of letters asking for more about Quincy and the Mason's Corner folks. This sequel, published in 1909 and illustrated by Henry Roth, answers those letters. Pidgin dedicates it to his daughter Dora.

Quincy returns in public life, taking an oath before representatives and an audience of eminent men and women to support the constitutions of his state and his country. Around that public Quincy, the familiar village folk gather again, with new faces, including a pretty girl in picturesque Italian costume. The book is a warm, old-fashioned sequel, written for readers who did not want to leave Mason's Corner.
8743-mary-schweidler-the-amber-witch-the:
Wilhelm Meinhold's The Amber Witch, translated by Lady Duff Gordon, presents itself as the most interesting trial for witchcraft ever known. Printed from an imperfect manuscript by Abraham Schweidler, pastor of Coserow on the island of Usedom. The story is told by the pastor himself, in chapters that begin with imperial soldiers robbing him, breaking into the church, and stealing the sacred vessels. Hunger follows: his last cow falls dead, wolves having devoured the rest, with suspicion falling on Lizzie.

Mary, the pastor's daughter, stands accused of witchcraft, and the manuscript form lets Meinhold blur history and fiction, a trick that fooled many early readers. The novel, first published in 1846, became famous as a supposed true record before its fictional nature was admitted. Readers get a gripping witch trial narrative, and a lesson in how a well-made forgery can pass for history.
9700-i-beo-wulf-an-anglo-saxon-poem-ii-t:
Beowulf appears here in a second Harrison and Sharp text, corrected from the fourth edition and signed with notes by KTH. The base version presents the poem as printed, in Latin-1 text, keeping old accents save y-circumflex, now y-acute. Errors fixed only where the book contradicts itself, as when glossary quotes differ from the main text. Deliberate editorial choices stand, even where scholars now disagree.

A full list of changes closes the file, so a reader can trace each fix. The Fight at Finnsburh fragment rides beside the epic. A reader gets a careful, transparent Beowulf for study, with its editor's hand shown, not hidden.
9701-i-be-owulf-an-anglo-saxon-poem-ii-t:
Beowulf, the Old English hero poem, appears here in the Harrison and Sharp edition, revised from its fourth printing. The text keeps the printed original's accents, with small corrections where the book contradicts itself. Notes flag problems that might confuse a reader, rather than silently fixing them. The Fight at Finnsburh, a fragment of a second old poem, rides with Beowulf in this volume.

Readers meet Beowulf's fights with Grendel, Grendel's mother, and the dragon, in a text made for study. Glossary notes aid the hard words. A reader gets a scholar's Beowulf, faithful to its source, and a rare fragment beside the main epic.
a-celtic-psaltery-being-mainly-rendering: Alfred Perceval Graves renders Irish and Welsh poetry into English verse in this Celtic psaltery. Its Irish poems include the Isle of the Happy, the wisdom of King Cormac, lays of the saints, and the breastplate of St. Patrick. Welsh pieces follow, with songs of praise and legend from the Celtic tradition. The collection offers English readers the music and spirit of old Celtic verse.
an-enquiry-into-the-obligations-of-chris: William Carey enquires into the obligations of Christians to use means for the conversion of the heathens, weighing the religious state of the nations, past efforts, and what further efforts are practicable. The tract became the charter of the modern missionary movement. Carey's calm, reasoned plea changed how Protestant churches saw the wider world.
britannica-1911-bellows-albert-f:
Albert F. Bellows (1829–1883) was an American landscape painter born at Milford, Massachusetts. He studied architecture first, then turned to painting and worked in Paris and at the Royal Academy in Antwerp. He painted a great deal in England during his career.

Bellows belonged to the National Academy of Design and the American Water Color Society, and held honorary place in Belgium’s water-colour society. Early on he painted scenes of daily life in oils, but after 1865 water-colour took over and landscape became his ground. Known works include “Afternoon in Surrey,” “Sunday in Devonshire,” shown at Philadelphia, and “The Parsonage.” He died at Auburndale in 1883.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-felician-sist:
The Felician Sisters were founded at Warsaw on 21 November 1855. Mother Mary Angela founded them under the direction of Father Honorat, a Capuchin. Suppressed by the Russian government in 1864, they moved to Cracow. There the congregation grew to forty-four houses in the Cracow province.

In the United States, where they arrived in 1874, they soon formed two provinces. They counted 820 sisters, 100 novices, and 168 postulants at the time. Their 87 schools taught some 36,700 pupils across many states. They also ran five orphanages, homes for the aged, an emigrant home, and a day nursery.
doe-osti-1686142-scale-up-of-electrode-c:
Cooperative final report CRD-17-00687, issued in February 2026 by the National Laboratory of the Rockies, has Michael Ulsh as its laboratory contact. The partner, Peroxygen Systems, makes hydrogen peroxide on site with an electrolyzer rather than shipping strong peroxide from central plants. The work dealt with scaling that machine toward customer pilot tests.

Three scale up tasks fill the report. One tested roll to roll coating of electrode material for cells of two sizes. A second built an in line check for coating quality during production. A third ran cells and stacks in place to test and tune the flow field design, the channels that move fluids through the cell.
doe-osti-17084209-70-capacitor-zx-marx-d:
Design report SAND2026-26920 from William Brooks, Amanda Norris, and a large Sandia team covers a 70 capacitor Marx generator for the ZX upgrade of the Z pulsed power facility. A Marx bank stores energy in capacitors, then dumps it in one fast pulse. The ZX goal is doubling stored energy from 20 megajoules on the current machine to 40 megajoules.

Each of the 36 Marx units, plus spares, grows from 60 to 70 capacitors, with higher capacity units charged to 95 kilovolts instead of 85. Chapters detail column spacing, hanging straps, spreaders, and the Marx testbed. A second charge assesses facility changes needed for assembly, upkeep, testbed use, and Z operation.
doe-osti-17091589-assessment-of-242pu-n-:
Nicolas Schunck, Anton Tonchev, Alex Tuckey, and Randal Vogt of Lawrence Livermore assess how plutonium 242 splits under slow neutrons and under gamma rays, in a report dated October 2026. When the nucleus fissions, prompt neutrons and prompt photons fly out at once. Their counts and energies feed reactor and stockpile calculations, so the values must be trustworthy.

Three fission event codes were run side by side: FETA, built on Hauser Feshbach statistics; GEF, a rule based model; and FREYA, built on Weisskopf Ewing statistics. Each chapter shows fragment yields, neutron counts, and photon output from one code. FREYA results were left out of the final determination, and the assessment weighs the other two against data.
doe-osti-17135839-moscato-development-an:
Haomin Yuan, Benjamin Li, Nadish Saini, and Argonne colleagues report fiscal 2026 progress on MOSCATO, a simulation tool for molten salt reactors, in report ANL/NSE-26/28. MOSCATO couples fluid flow, heat transfer, mass transfer, chemistry, electrochemistry, and corrosion in one framework. Salt systems need that coupling because each process feeds the others.

New this year is mass transfer across gas liquid interfaces, built on a level set method that tracks bubble surfaces. The capability matters for tritium movement, gas sparging, and gas chemistry in salt. Tests covered gas exchange around moving bubbles across flow speeds. Other work updated the bubbly flow solver, validated a two channel corrosion model, and added noble metal deposition. Oxygen entry experiments served as a validation case.
doe-osti-2572406-construction-of-approxi:
Brookhaven technical note BNL-228410-2025-TECH, also numbered NSLSII-ASD-TN-426 and dated July 2025, presents a construction method by Yongjun Li, Derong Xu, and Yue Hao. The subject is approximate invariants, quantities that stay nearly constant as particles circulate in a ring accelerator. Exact invariants rarely exist for realistic, non-integrable systems, yet long-term stability depends on finding good stand-ins.

The method exploits a special form of the one-turn map, written as a square matrix. Invariants are then built order by order as polynomials of growing degree. When the authors score an invariant on simulation data, its wobble turns out to measure how chaotic the motion is. Shrinking that wobble widens the dynamic aperture, the region of stable long-term motion. The note applies the construction to a modern ring-based accelerator and frames it for accelerator physics use.
doe-osti-2572417-high-average-current-hv:
Brookhaven technical note BNL-228424-2025-TECH, also numbered EIC-ADD-TN-126 and dated July 2025, lays out the high-voltage design of an electron gun for the Electron-Ion Collider. Lead author E. Wang and a large Brookhaven team, with partners at Dielectric Sciences, address the gun for the collider's hadron cooler. Cooling keeps hadron beams tight enough to hit the target luminosity of ten to the thirty-fourth per square centimeter per second.

For an energy-recovery-linac cooler, the gun must deliver 98.5 milliamps of average current. It must also hold normalized emittance under two millimeter-milliradians and bunch charges up to 2.5 nanocoulombs. The design runs at 500 kilovolts, with conditioning headroom to 600. Distinctive features include inverted ceramic insulators at this voltage, an actively cooled cathode using fluorinert fluid, and large single-crystal multi-alkali cathodes grown on silicon carbide. An overview of cooling approaches for the collider rounds out the note.
doe-osti-2573951-inclusive-shared-solar-:
Final technical report DE-EE0009008, from the National Association of State Energy Officials under Sandy Fazeli and covering March 2020 to October 2024, reports the Inclusive Shared Solar Initiative. Community solar lets households subscribe to a share of a local solar project instead of installing rooftop panels. It is often the only solar route for renters and for homes with poor roofs, yet low- and moderate-income households were being left out.

The initiative worked through state energy offices and the NEADA network. An advisory group shaped a request for proposals, promoted in a November 2020 webinar, to recruit state implementation partners. The report reviews what blocks poorer subscribers: subscription costs, contract terms and fees, and weak outreach. State designs that help include capacity carve-outs, discounted rates, consumer protections, and developer incentives. A December 2023 roundtable in Madison, Wisconsin, took up financing and partnerships for scaling the model.
doe-osti-2580493-optimized-v1g-and-v2g-e:
CRADA final report LBNL-2001687, dated July 30, 2025, reports a vehicle-to-grid demonstration at Marine Corps Air Station Miramar in San Diego. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory partnered with the Naval Facilities Engineering Command, with Douglas Black and Mick Wasco as technical contacts. Six bidirectional electric vans joined the station's building-scale microgrid, alongside a 30 kilowatt rooftop solar array and a 250 kilowatt carport array.

The vans, VIA Motors vehicles chosen for passenger and cargo duty, charged and discharged under central control with the other resources. Three things were to be proven. Bidirectional vehicles can complement fixed batteries in a microgrid while still working as fleet vehicles. Managed charging, one-way or two-way, cuts charging costs and shaves demand. And combined resources can sell services into grid programs. The California Energy Commission funded the project; no subject inventions resulted.
doe-osti-2584742-improved-decay-data-for:
Isabel Hernandez reports new nuclear decay data in LLNL report LLNL-TR-2008067, dated July 2025. The work covers three long-lived fission products: neodymium-147, silver-111, and europium-156. Decay data of this kind fix the odds of each decay path and the strength of the gamma rays given off, values that many nuclear studies rely on.

The team has published exact gamma ray strengths for the decay of neodymium-147 in Physical Review C. For europium-156, new values cut the error bars on the strongest gamma rays by a factor of ten or more, and a journal paper is in draft. For silver-111, a beta-gamma method gave a clean spectrum and a half-life of 7.42 days. That value sits close to the 7.45 and 7.473 days found in past work.
doe-osti-2586512-transformational-sorben:
Ravi Jain, president of InnoSepra, submitted this final report in December 2024 for Department of Energy grant DE-FE00031722, which ran from May 2019 through August 2024. The project built a sorbent-based process meant to cut the cost of capturing carbon dioxide substantially. Sorbents are solid materials that soak up the gas and release it again when regenerated.

The task list traces the full path from idea to pilot plant. The team screened candidate materials with literature review, computing tools, and lab measurements, then ran breakthrough and cyclic tests on the best of them. Process simulation and a first feasibility study followed. A pilot unit was designed, costed, built, shipped, and installed, and pilot-scale testing occupies a long chapter of its own. The report closes with a final techno-economic analysis and a technology gap assessment.
doe-osti-2589175-using-solid-particles-a:
Zhiwen Ma of the National Renewable Energy Laboratory is the technical contact for this CRADA final report, NREL/TP-5700-96587, dated September 2025, with Christine Hrenya of the University of Colorado Boulder sharing credit. It covers Project 3, Modification 2 of CRADA CRD-12-00480. That is the BRIDGE project. It built granular flow and heat transfer simulation tools for a solar power design that replaces molten salt with hot solid particles.

Particles run hotter than salt and store heat cheaply. The catch is predicting how a flowing bed of grains gives up its heat. NREL developed a particle system built around an enclosed receiver. Colorado's team modeled flow and heat transfer for it. NREL supplied the design, operating conditions, and test results for verification. One model detail stands out. Each particle is treated as wrapped in a thin interstitial fluid lens. Where that lens touches a wall, conduction through it carries the heat.
doe-osti-2589498-numerical-investigation:
National Renewable Energy Laboratory final report NREL/TP-5700-97038 closes cooperative project CRD-23-23742 on a small water power device. Technical contact Thanh Toan Tran worked with a Florida Atlantic University team on an undershot waterwheel fitted with a flow concentrator, a shroud that squeezes current onto the blades. The turbine is meant to feed small autonomous recharge stations at sea.

Computer flow studies varied blade count, wheel shape, submerged depth, tip speed ratio, and concentrator shape. Runs covered plain current and combined wave-plus-current conditions. Goals were more power and lower structural loads at once. The university team supplied the base design, size limits, and safe clearances between blade tips and the concentrator. Results give the designers a ranked set of changes to build and test in water next.
doe-osti-2589924-acoustophoretic-additiv:
University of Washington final report on award DE-EE0009112 covers a printing method that uses sound to structure battery electrodes. Corie Cobb led the work, with Matthew Begley at the University of California, Santa Barbara. Work ran from September 2020 to March 2025. Sound waves in a liquid ink push active particles into patterns as the electrode is printed, giving 3D structure without slow layer carving.

Tasks set electrode and material targets, matched inks to the acoustic process, and validated a nozzle for line patterns. A chamber design for grid patterns was modeled and then tested. Quality checks stitched microscope images across a 25 by 50 millimeter area and scored line breaks over 0.5 millimeters. Patterned electrodes aim to move lithium faster, raising power without giving up capacity.
doe-osti-2997485-fy2025-status-report-mo:
Savannah River National Laboratory status report SRNL-STI-2025-00588, by Thanh-Tam Truong, dated September 2025, updates a leak test program running since 2004. The subject is the rubber O-ring seals of the Model 9975 shipping package, which carries nuclear material. Seals age in storage, and the lab bakes mock containment vessels at high heat to age them fast and find failure times.

Seventy fixtures with the original Viton GLT rings were heated between 200 and 450 degrees Fahrenheit; fourteen more with the substitute GLT-S grade ran from 2008 at 200 to 400 degrees. Every GLT fixture aged at 350 degrees or above eventually leaked. At 300 degrees, eight fixtures failed after 2.8 to 5.7 years. Two retired survivors reheated to 350 degrees failed within three and nine months. Storage limits for the fleet rest on this record.
doe-osti-2997585-cold-spray-field-deploy:
Hanford contractor report RPP-RPT-66087, by Stephanie Doll, Jose Avila, and Rogeiro Renteria, dated September 2025, evaluates a robotic coating job inside a giant waste tank. Double-shell tank 241-AN-105 holds radioactive waste at the Hanford Site, and its annulus floor needed a protective metal coating. Cold spray, which blasts metal powder at high speed so it sticks without melting, was applied in July 2025.

Work was a joint effort with VRC Metal Systems and Robotic Technologies of Tennessee, using a wall-crawling robot and a Raptor spray system. Equipment tables log each part, from powder feeders to the crawler's heater module, with serial numbers and revisions. Ultrasonic testing and an independent tank integrity firm verified the work. At 199 pages, the volume is the field record: preparation, application photos, and the checks that closed the job.
doe-osti-2997988-resdesign-resilient-by-:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory final project report, dated September 2025, presents ResDesign, a platform for testing whether control systems survive attacks and failures. Lead authors Sumit Purohit, Thiagarajan Ramachandran, and Oceane Bel, with a large team, built the tool for cyber-physical systems such as power grids, where software and hardware fail together.

Use cases include worst-case impact assessment and risk review of existing installations. Stress testing against a 3,000-bus grid model exposed a practical trap: a timestep setting in both the power flow and generator models can crash the simulation when set badly. Setting both to 10 milliseconds kept the large model running correctly. Future work pairs the team with the GridLAB-D developers. Engineers gain a test bench where resilience claims can be rehearsed before they are believed.
doe-osti-2997990-progress-towards-nqa-1-:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL/NSE-25/81 tracks a year of work toward NQA-1 quality certification for Cardinal, the laboratory's coupled heat and flow simulation code built on the NekRS solver. Authors Nadish Saini, Maximiliano Dalinger, Kalin Kiesling, and co-authors report fiscal year 2025 progress. NQA-1 is the nuclear quality standard a code must meet before its results can anchor licensing cases.

Verification chapters work case by case through both the wrapper code and the solver beneath it. Test problems include turbulent channel flow, a classic curved-flow solution case, low-speed compressible flow, laminar pipe and channel runs, a turbulent pipe case, conjugate heat transfer, and a moving cylinder. Each case checks solver output against a known answer. The report gives quality reviewers an itemized trail of what has been proven and what remains.
doe-osti-2999316-moscato-development-and:
Haomin Yuan, Nadish Saini, Dezhi Dai and co-workers at Argonne National Laboratory report fiscal 2025 progress on the MOSCATO code, in ANL/NSE-25/40. MOSCATO, short for Molten Salt Chemistry and Transport, simulates molten salt systems all at once: fluid flow, heat, mass movement, chemistry, electrochemistry and alloy corrosion. Molten salt reactors need that joined view, since their fuel and coolant are the same hot liquid.

The year's headline work was two-phase flow, salt plus gas bubbles. A level-set method, which tracks the boundary between phases, was improved and checked against helium bubbles rising in still FLiNaK salt. Computed rise speeds and bubble shapes matched the filmed tests well. A bubbly flow solver also got first checks in a vertical pipe. New mass transfer correlations support tracking tritium across such flows. The report sets out validation done and the coupled problems next in line.
doe-osti-3000708-vacuum-baking-provides-:
Sarah Matt, Cheng Saw, Bill McLean and L Dinh of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report in LLNL-TR-2013021, dated October 2025, on taming a reactive material with a bake. Lithium hydride is a salt-like solid that corrodes fast: seconds in room air grow a lithium hydroxide skin a few hundred nanometres thick. That skin later releases gas and moisture, troubling the sealed systems where lithium hydride serves.

Warm-pressed disks, 12.7 centimetres across, were polished, aired to grow measured corrosion layers of 240 to 540 nanometres, then heated to 470-490 kelvin under high vacuum. Baking converted the hydroxide skin into a lithium oxide cover instead. Infrared spectroscopy watched the layers during heating holds of up to 150 hours, and a separate vacuum technique compared gas release from baked and unbaked samples. The baked surface re-formed only a thin hydroxide layer on brief re-exposure. Vacuum baking thus buys cleaner, quieter storage behaviour.
doe-osti-3002665-magnetic-bearing-pumps-:
Alexander Melin, Matthew Vernacchia, Vandana Rallabandi, and Emilian Popov close CRADA project NFE-22-09139 in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/3751. Its title page is dated September 2024. The project designed pumps that circulate molten salt inside fusion energy devices. Magnetic bearings float the pump shaft without contact, avoiding seals and lubricants that hot, corrosive salt would destroy.

Fusion concepts that blanket the reactor in molten salt need such pumps to move the salt through heat exchangers. The report covers the pump design work and its supporting analysis, from motor cooling to insulation materials rated for high temperature. References reach from compact fusion facility studies to ceramic insulation data. A contact-free pump that survives molten salt service removes one practical obstacle between fusion pilot plants and steady operation.
doe-osti-3004246-design-and-development-:
Colby Winters, a UC Davis master's student, presents a capstone design report hosted by Lawrence Livermore, dated November 2025 and marked draft. The project designs a handling frame assembly table for the National Ignition Facility sustainment program. Sustainment is the multi-decade effort to keep the giant laser facility's hardware serviceable. A dedicated table supports safe assembly of the frames that move facility components.

The design passed through a requirements review in November 2024, a conceptual design review in January 2025, and a final design review in June 2025. The report compiles that progression as the capstone record. Its department page is dated March 2026, reflecting the academic calendar. Capstone reports like this one give the host laboratory a documented design package while giving the student a real engineering deliverable.
doe-osti-3011516-confinement-exploiting-:
Arrays of cross flow turbines that exploit confinement can cut the levelized cost of energy by at least half, according to the ConExT final report from the University of Washington. The work ran under award DE-AR0001441. Brian Polagye led a team with the University of Wisconsin Madison, the National Renewable Energy Laboratory, and Oberon Insights. The project period ran from August 2021 to June 2025. Gains over conventional staggered layouts were shown in scale model experiments.

Simulation extended the results toward full scale Reynolds numbers. An integrated techno economic model applied control co design. It balanced power output, component sizing, and structural loads. One milestone, a smart sensing algorithm for control strategy search, was not completed after review with the programme manager.
doe-osti-3012849-polk-power-station-ngcc:
Prepared by Sargent and Lundy for Tampa Electric Company, this front end engineering design package covers a carbon capture plant at Polk Power Station Unit 2. The unit is a natural gas combined cycle plant in Florida. The hosted text is not a narrative report. It is the engineering deliverable set itself: process flow diagrams, plant arrangement drawings, a project schedule, and a permitting matrix dated January 9, 2024.

The diagrams trace two carbon capture trains through absorbers, strippers, a reclaimer, and carbon dioxide compressors. Wash water and cooling systems are drawn in. The project execution schedule lays out the FEED study and a permitting track of about 335 days inside a timeline running from 2024 to 2029. The permitting matrix lists state and federal approvals. Among them is the Class VI well permit needed to inject captured carbon dioxide underground.
doe-osti-3013870-probabilistic-predictio:
Sandia report SAND2026-15526, by John Mersch, Vicente Romero, and Edmundo Corona, printed December 2025, documents blind predictions of fastener failure for the Sandia Mechanics Challenge. In the challenge, modelers received calibration data and had to predict, before seeing test results, how bolted joints would fail. The exercise exposes how well uncertainty methods work when the answer is genuinely unknown.

The team used the Discrete-Direct calibration and uncertainty propagation approach, which suits cases where only a few replicate tests can sample a whole population's variability. Material calibration covered aluminum stress-strain behavior at 25 and 100 degrees Celsius, plus notched tension and hat specimen tests. Post-blind chapters recalibrate against the revealed experiments and draw lessons about element size and failure modeling.
doe-osti-3015378-strategic-energy-plan-c:
A strategic energy plan for Key West, Florida is laid out in a Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory report dated January 2026, written through the ETIPP partnership program. The island city, part of ETIPP's fourth cohort, aims to improve efficiency and independence with local resources and to harden itself against flooding and hurricanes. Amanda Krelling led the author team.

Four focus areas organize the plan: energy efficiency across municipal, homes, and commercial buildings; more local generation; stronger resilience for critical infrastructure and residents; and electric transport with reliable charging. Appendices benchmark single-family homes, score efficiency measures, and map solar potential on homes. One practical finding: a secure power supply feature built into certain inverters offers limited backup at minimal extra cost, but only when an inverter is being replaced anyway.
doe-osti-3018623-requirements-descriptio:
Micheal A Smith of Argonne National Laboratory wrote this requirements document, ANL/NSE-26/1, for DASSH-F. DASSH is the laboratory's subchannel thermal-hydraulics code for fast reactor analysis. It sits inside the Argonne Reactor Code System set of codes. Commercial users run the code under license, and licensing raises a question. Which inputs and outputs must be verified before a result can be trusted? Smith reviewed the code's input and output files to answer it.

Output tables were sorted into those worth verifying and those not verifiable or not important. The power balance is his example of the second class: useful diagnostically, impossible to verify in detail. From that sorting came a table of verification tasks. The document gives licensees and reviewers a checklist. Instead of arguing case by case, both sides can point to the same list. That is the function of a requirements description in regulated software.
doe-osti-3019236-nrel-validation-of-s3-2:
Michael Kempe, Vahan Gevorgian, Timothy Silverman, Joseph Berry, and Axel Palmstrom of the National Laboratory of the Rockies wrote this CRADA final report, NLR/TP-5K00-96482, February 2026. The partner was First Solar. The task was validating its new module packaging, designated S3.2 and S3.3. Accelerated testing came first under the original agreement. A follow-up modification moved modules outdoors. A small grid-tied system with an inverter was monitored for degradation, with observation planned over five years.

A third modification widened the scope. The laboratory helped investigate performance shortfalls seen in certain products at First Solar test arrays. Electroluminescence imaging runs through the evidence: cracked cells show clearly in some systems, clean images in others. For a manufacturer, independent validation separates a packaging problem from a site problem. The report delivers that separation, with the outdoor record still running on its five-year clock.
doe-osti-3019931-cost-effectiveness-of-l:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory report ORNL/TM-2025/4317 is the final report for a CRADA project with Cummins Inc. on laser powder bed fusion, a metal 3D printing method, for heavy duty parts. Peeyush Nandwana and five co-authors studied grade 300 maraging steel, a steel often used for tool inserts. The question was whether printing could be both fast and good enough to be cost effective in production.

The team printed test pieces on an AddUp FormUp 350 system using two sets of process settings for the inside and the surface of each part. The faster settings raised the deposition rate by 21 percent over the standard settings. Both settings kept porosity below 0.2 percent of the measured area. Cummins also ran builds on a GE Concept Laser M2 system to tune aging heat treatments for maximum hardness.
doe-osti-3020400-fission-evaluation-tool:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory document LLNL-TR-2013408, by Nicolas Schunck, is the living manual for FETA, a Python package that computes what comes out of nuclear fission. When a heavy nucleus splits, the fragments carry excitation energy and spin, then emit neutrons and photons. Measuring the initial fragments directly is impossible, so evaluators must predict their properties from models.

FETA assembles those models in one modular framework. It calculates fission yields, prompt and delayed neutron and photon spectra, level densities, gamma-strength functions, and neutron transmission coefficients. Users can swap any built-in model for their own file supplying the same quantities. The document defines each observable and the physics behind it, serving both evaluators who need fission inputs and researchers testing new models of the fission process.
doe-osti-3020508-wind-lidar-operations-a:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory guide LLNL-TR-2013882, by atmospheric scientist Sonia Wharton, documents the wind data collected during the Tundra Pigeon field experiment. Livermore deployed a ZX-300 profiling lidar, an instrument that tracks drifting aerosols with light to derive wind speed and direction. For this tracer experiment, the lidar profiled winds from 10 to 200 meters above ground, with an onboard sensor logging conditions at 1 meter.

The guide describes both measurement sites: open grassland at Site 1 and a second site near a cluster of small buildings at ground zero. It walks through each experiment day's weather. On the first morning, winds near the ground averaged about 3.1 meters per second with little shear. The document serves as the reference for anyone using the Tundra Pigeon wind dataset.
doe-osti-3021489-design-and-development-:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2016401, by Colby Winters, dated March 2026, documents the design of a work table built for assembling the handling frames of the National Ignition Facility's blast shields. The report doubles as Winters's UC Davis mechanical engineering master's capstone project. Blast shield handling frames are heavy, precise hardware, and the table had to support assembly work while surviving an earthquake without tipping or sliding.

The design uses a large bent aluminum sheet top reinforced with welded stiffener bars. Legs bolt to L-brackets anchored to the floor as seismic restraints, and side and rear bracing adds stiffness against seismic loads. Storage troughs along each side hold assembly pins and center bars, cleaning supplies, and a torque wrench. The document records the requirements, the structure, and the reasoning behind each feature.
doe-osti-3021941-systems-to-atoms-s2a-en:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory full technical report LLNL-TR-2011755, by Sneha Akhade and Matthew McNenly, dated March 2026, reports the Systems-to-Atoms (S2A) project, grant GS 23-ERD-016, on hydrogen delivery. Hydrogen is awkward to move: compressing or liquefying it costs energy, so chemical carriers are attractive. S2A connects the scales, from catalyst atoms to full refueling stations, so choices at one scale are checked against costs at the others.

The worked example is the formic acid delivery pathway. The framework calculates catalyst requirements, unit costs, and net station costs across material, component, and system scales, under varying temperature and pressure. Machine learning surrogates trained on those cross-scale parameters then search for co-optimized designs under future scenarios, such as stations needing higher capacity as hydrogen demand grows. The report presents the framework as reusable for other carriers and climates of demand.
doe-osti-3025759-an-entirely-wood-floor-:
Brandon E Ross of Clemson University led award DE-AR0001640, running September 2022 to September 2025, reported March 18, 2026, with five co-investigators. The team designed a floor system built entirely of wood. Wood floors store biogenic carbon for the life of the building, and a system designed for disassembly can be taken apart and rebuilt instead of landfilled, which is the project's closing promise.

Milestone results are candid about the hard parts. In isolated tests, about half of measured vibrations exceeded office acceleration comfort thresholds, a result blamed on the test boundary conditions and later resolved in system-level testing. Sound testing split: airborne performance met its threshold, while impact sound only passed once finish layers were installed. A comprehensive review then cleared the design to move to system-level work.
doe-osti-3028176-high-resolution-fault-c: Kai Gao of Los Alamos National Laboratory issued these slides as LA-UR-26-22418 on March 26, 2026, on high-resolution fault characterization for judging induced earthquake hazards. The hosted text is only the slide captions. They compare geological fault readings from seismic images made by a conventional AI model against a multimodal AI model that also uses seismicity information. Beside them sit examples of random realistic geological models from the team's multi-randomization method, published as Gao and Chen, 2026, in Computers and Geosciences. No fuller text accompanies the figures.
doe-osti-3133135-industrial-assessment-c:
Michael R. Muller of Rutgers University Center for Advanced Energy Systems closes award DE-EE0008278 in this final report, covering February 2018 to August 2024. Muller served as Technical Field Manager for the Industrial Assessment Centers. These centers, hosted at universities, send student teams into small and mid-sized factories to find energy savings. A field manager keeps quality up across the network and links the centers to Energy Department priorities.

Duties spanned seven tasks: coordinating center operations, reviewing every assessment report, training staff and students, and running the program websites and databases. The team also built resource guides for factories nationwide and pushed an accredited energy engineering degree. The 2022 directors meeting in Denver drew about 75 people, with talks on heat pumps, hydrogen, and cyber security.
doe-osti-3363530-creation-of-speed-of-so:
Arthur Rodgers and Eric Matzel of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory and Mark Leidig of Applied Research Associates describe how speed-of-sound exercise data are built for technical nuclear forensics (LLNL-TR-2016281, January 2026). These exercises simulate a nuclear detonation in a U.S. city, and the speed-of-sound signals are the air blast overpressure and ground shock motions that air blast, infrasound, and seismic sensors would record.

The report walks through simulation, validation, preparation, and verification of the synthetic signals. Players, who know nothing about the device, feed the data to the Integrated Yield Determination Tool to estimate yield and height or depth of burst. The tool keys on the impulse of the first seismic P-wave and the first positive overpressure pulse.
doe-osti-3364386-resstock-measure-docume:
National Laboratory of the Rockies report NLR/TP-5500-96635 documents two heating upgrades for ResStock, the lab's model of the U.S. housing stock. Katelyn Stenger, Philip White, Andrew Parker, Jeff Maguire, Joe Robertson, and Sinoun Phoung wrote it. The upgrades swap existing furnaces for a propane furnace rated at 95 percent AFUE or a fuel oil furnace at 88 percent AFUE. AFUE measures how much fuel energy becomes usable heat over a season.

Documentation explains how the measures translate home characteristics into simulation inputs through the OpenStudio-HPXML workflow. Both furnaces are modeled as forced-air systems in homes with central ducts. Analysts running ResStock 2025 Release 1 use the document to reproduce the upgrade results and see exactly which assumptions drive them. It is a methods record for a public modeling tool.
doe-osti-3374178-tailored-silicone-netwo:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2020120, by Jake Grondz of the University of Oregon and dated June 2026, studies how the inner network of a silicone elastomer sets its strength. Silicones cured by hydrosilylation often cure unevenly, leaving loose ends and weak spots in the crosslink network that limit toughness. Grondz asks whether tailoring that network on purpose, with brush-like polymer chains and multi-armed linkers, can reinforce the material.

The work builds several network structures and tunes the mix of parts for each. For two structures, the share of functional groups from a vinyl-rich part was held at ratios of 0.5 and 0.1 against the multi-functional part, chosen to favor the wanted structure and limit side reactions. The author notes that nuclear magnetic resonance work is still needed to find the true best mix, since one dense linker made the material highly sensitive to small mix changes.
doe-osti-3374309-seasonal-spatial-vertic:
Department of Energy Atmospheric Radiation Measurement report DOE/SC-ARM-26-016, dated June 2026, covers a field campaign on how new particle formation changes with height, place, and season. Its authors are Jie Zhang, Fan Yu, Chongai Kuang, and Darielle Dexheimer. New particles form in the air from gases and then grow, affecting clouds and air quality, but most records come from ground level. The team flew a tethered balloon system carrying a scanning particle sizer to profile the air column.

Flights ran during deployment periods at the Bankhead National Forest site and the CoURAGE campaign. The balloon records showed strong shifts in particle size patterns with height, plus several recurring aerosol regimes. The authors conclude that total particle counts and boundary layer height alone cannot describe the column; size-resolved profiles reveal stored layers aloft, mixing, and season-driven formation working together.
doe-osti-3374325-tes-modelling-microbes-:
A final technical report for Department of Energy award DE-SC0021022 covers August 2020 to August 2025 work on soil microbes after boreal forest fires. Thea Whitman at the University of Wisconsin-Madison led it, with Benjamin Sulman of Oak Ridge National Laboratory. Boreal wildfires move huge amounts of carbon, yet models treat the soil microbes that drive post-fire carbon release only crudely. The team asked whether linking microbe makeup and activity to burn severity and plant cover could sharpen those models.

Field and lab work fed the CORPSE soil model, which tracks carbon, organisms, roots, and soil protection together. Study stands covered upland jack pine and upland spruce across burn severities. The grant trained two early-career scientists, produced two peer-reviewed papers with two more pending, and supported over twenty talks, while building joint work between university and national lab researchers.
doe-osti-3375393-design-and-development-:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory report LLNL-TR-2018388, by Colby Winters and dated June 2026, documents a custom assembly table for the National Ignition Facility. The report began as a UC Davis master's capstone project, advised by Dr. La Saponara. The table assembles and stores the handling frames that carry blast shields for the laser's optics. Those frames are costly and easy to scratch, so the work surface had to protect them at each step.

The loaded table weighs about twelve hundred pounds. It splits into three parts: a drawer, the table frame, and top fixturing. The drawer measures eighty-six by forty-four by eleven inches. It rides on store-bought slides and is built from 6061-T6 aluminum, picked for strength at low weight and cost. Delrin guides cradle each frame in storage. The soft plastic keeps metal edges from scarring the frames during loading.
doe-osti-3377550-analysis-of-power-elect:
Technical report NLR/TP-5700-93489, dated July 2026, compares power electronics for wave energy converters whose input swings over a range. Alec Schnabel, Yeongrack Son, Kumaraguru Prabakar, and Ramanathan Thiagarajan ran the study at the National Laboratory of the Rockies. Ocean waves arrive in bursts, not a push. The converter between a wave device and the grid must cope with that swing. Pick a topology and energy is lost at both calm and storm ends.

Simulations drive the comparison. The team modeled a six-foot hexagonal float with a winch-style power take-off. One damping setting held across all wave profiles, so each topology faced the sea. A 10-kilowatt permanent magnet generator anchors the machine side. Its ratings are tabled: stator resistance of 0.16 ohms and a 25-amp peak current among them. Both machine and electronics ran in Simulink. Output and efficiency scores decide the ranking.
doe-osti-3379844-biodegradable-biocompos:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory CRADA final report ORNL/TM-2026/4640, dated June 2026, describes a biodegradable biocomposite feedstock for large-scale additive manufacturing. The work was done with Mitsubishi Chemical America. Ten authors are printed, led by Soydan Ozcan, Caitlyn Clarkson, and Halil Tekinalp. The feedstock is built on polybutylene succinate, a biobased polyester used in agriculture and packaging. It is blended with polylactic acid and wood flour.

Wood flour, used at up to 30 percent by weight, improves printability and stiffness and cuts cost. But it weakens tensile strength. A chain extender was added to bind the blend back together. The team printed a demonstration mold for precast concrete catch basins. They cast 750 pounds of concrete in it, and the mold survived. Aerobic testing showed 40 percent biodegradation after 90 days. That is well beyond incumbent biobased feedstocks.
doe-osti-3384917-biodegradable-biocompos: Clarkson, Copenhaver, Tekinalp and colleagues take on the plastic problem in 3-D printing. Their project builds new biocomposites that microbes can digest — materials grown from plants, not pumped from oil — for printing at industrial scale. If it works, tomorrow's printed goods won't outlive us in a dump.
doe-osti-3412370-development-of-function:
Penn State closes award DE-EE0009647 with a final report on new electrolytes for lithium-sulfur battery cells. Donghai Wang and Guoxing Li led the project. The reporting period ran from January 1, 2022 to December 31, 2025. Lithium-sulfur cells promise high capacity but fade fast.

One new electrolyte, called electrolyte A in the text, gave about 1100 milliamp-hours per gram at a slow rate. After forming cycles, cells still gave up to 730 at a faster discharge rate. Cycling stayed stable in the tests shown. Better electrolytes could make light, high-capacity batteries real for vehicles.
doe-osti-3422488-polk-power-station-co2-:
Final report on the Polk Power Station carbon capture project, under award DE-CD0000007 from the Office of Clean Energy Demonstrations, tracks design work through 2025. Nathan Dilport is the named author in the evidence record. The hosted text is a short monthly progress account, so this note stays close to that scope.

Work in mid-2025 covered sequestration site review and process design updates. Reviews closed on foundations, piping, ductwork, and electrical layout. Data sheets for process and carbon dioxide pumps were under review. A 30 percent review of the 3D model was complete. The project shows early build steps for capture at a working plant.
further-adventures-of-quincy-adams-sawye:
Charles Felton Pidgin's Further Adventures of Quincy Adams Sawyer and Mason's Corner Folks revisits the characters of his first success, eight years after its publication. Pidgin recalls hundreds of letters from unknown readers wishing to know more about Quincy and his neighbours.

Few sequels, Pidgin admits, are judged as interesting as the original, and an author tempts fate in writing one. Yet if a book's characters become friends, he argues, readers may fairly be invited to renew the acquaintance. The further adventures return to Mason's Corner and its folks, illustrated by Henry Roth. Readers who enjoyed Quincy will welcome the reunion.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-DolanJohnF_Dola:
An FBI memorandum dated February 12, 1968 came from the Bureau's Dallas office chief. It reports that John P. Dolan had been contacted by telephone by Jim Garrison, the New Orleans district attorney then investigating President Kennedy's assassination. Dolan told the Bureau he had declined to discuss the case with Garrison.

The memo matters because the FBI tracked Garrison's moves closely while publicly standing apart from his probe. A phone call to a Dallas man became a headquarters record within the Bureau. It shows the quiet monitoring that ran alongside the most public assassination investigation of the era.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HaleyGilbertF_H:
Harold Weisberg wrote to Gilbert F. Haley on February 16, 1974 and sent more than words. He enclosed damaged copies of his Whitewash series, the books that made his name as a Warren Report critic. The letter also invites Haley into a discussion of assassination finances.

Damaged stock was a working author's problem: books that could not be sold at full price still served as evidence in the right hands. Weisberg put his into the mail with an offer to talk money and cases. The letter shows him running his one-man publishing operation, copies, costs, and all.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KennedyJohnF_Ke:
Stewart Alsop wrote in the Saturday Evening Post on April 6, 1963 about a worried president. His subject was the crisis in President Kennedy's foreign policy. Alsop called it the collapse of Kennedy's grand design, the ambitious plan with which the young president had begun.

Seven months before Dallas, a leading columnist was already writing the administration as a design in ruins. Alsop had the access and the standing to say it in America's biggest magazine. The article preserves that judgment in full, a measure of how troubled Kennedy's presidency looked from inside Washington that spring.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-TaskForceDepart: On September 4, 1981, a researcher wrote to Ms. Madelyn Johnson in the Civil Division of the Department of Justice. The letter concerns JFK assassination task force records that could not be located. Missing files were a standing frustration for assassination researchers, who depended on government releases. The letter documents that paper chase, and the polite but firm pressure citizens put on the Justice Department.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cuba-cub:
Adlai Stevenson, the United States ambassador to the United Nations, played a central part in ending the Cuban Missile Crisis. Peter Kornbluh edited this briefing book, number 811, published in October 2022. Its subtitle says President John F. Kennedy sacrificed his most consequential crisis adviser.

Documents chart Stevenson's work in managing and resolving the crisis. His rule was blunt: blackmail and intimidation never, negotiation and sanity always. Yet his standing at home suffered after the settlement. The posting lets readers weigh his real contribution against the political price he paid for the deal that ended the standoff.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_nuclear-: President John F. Kennedy worried that Israel's Dimona reactor was meant for weapons, and he pushed hard for American inspections of the site. This briefing-book page presents the record of that pressure. Companion Archive volumes print his 1963 letters to Israeli leaders warning that American support could be jeopardized. The evidence here is the title alone, so this page serves as the short entry to that larger file on the strongest inspection demand a president ever made of Israel.
history-of-the-catholic-church-from-the-:
James MacCaffrey, an Irish priest and historian, wrote this history of the Catholic Church from the Renaissance to the French Revolution as a set of lectures with full reading lists. Volume one begins with the causes of the Reformation: the Renaissance itself, the state of the papacy, and the abuses reformers attacked. Chapter two turns to the religious revolution, Luther and Zwingli in Germany and beyond.

MacCaffrey writes from inside the Catholic tradition, citing Janssen, Pastor, and other Catholic historians alongside the Cambridge Modern History. His subject is how the Church met three centuries of upheaval: Protestant revolt, Catholic reform, and expanding missions. The bibliographies after each chapter make the volume a working textbook as much as a narrative.
home-life-of-the-lancashire-factory-folk:
Edwin Waugh wrote this record of Lancashire factory folk during the Cotton Famine. When American cotton stopped, the mills stopped with it. Waugh visited the operatives town by town for the papers. Blackburn and Preston fill the early chapters.

Wigan's streets show no striking sign of distress at first glance, he writes. A careful eye, though, finds more beggarly stragglers, awkward and hesitant. Wandering minstrels sing the wails of the workless poor. Letters and speeches on the famine, including Cobden's, close the book. Waugh gives the hungry north a voice in its own dialect and pride.
hume-history-of-england-1860-part-f:
Part F completes the 1860 Virtue edition of David Hume's History of England, closing the sixth and final part. Hume's history, published from 1754 to 1762, ends with the Glorious Revolution of 1688, where its seventy-one chapters stop. The philosopher from Edinburgh had written the book his whole century read.
