The final part brings the long contest of crown and parliament to its settlement. Hume's even hand and lucid style held readers who agreed with nothing else he wrote. For a hundred years, to know English history meant to have read Hume's version of it. Part F sets the last stone on that monument, and the set stands complete.
i-be-owulf-an-anglo-saxon-poem-ii-the-fi:
James Albert Harrison and Robert Sharp edited this scholarly Beowulf. The hosted text is their fourth edition, revised and corrected. It gives the Anglo-Saxon poem in its original tongue. The Fight at Finnsburh, a fragment, stands as the second piece.

A full glossary makes up much of the bulk. Word by word, it gives forms, meanings, and line numbers. Fallow horses go in emulation, one entry renders, for a racing phrase. Editors' notes flag where vowel lengths clash with later consensus. Deliberate choices are left untouched, the preface says, even where they look wrong. Students get the epic as a language monument, built for close study.
i-beo-wulf-an-anglo-saxon-poem-ii-the-fi:
James Albert Harrison and Robert Sharp prepared this edition of Beowulf for students. The hosted file presents their fourth edition in its original form. The Anglo-Saxon text of the poem fills the first part. The Finnsburh fragment, a broken battle lay, follows it.

The glossary glosses the poem's hard words one by one. To yield a foot's breadth to the mountain's warder, the dragon, is unpacked from a single compound. Signed notes mark spots where the text may confuse a reader. The preface owns that some vowel markings defy current consensus. This twin of its mate keeps the edition's first state, for comparison and study.
mary-schweidler-the-amber-witch-the-most:
Wilhelm Meinhold wrote The Amber Witch, in Lady Duff Gordon's English version. The title page calls it the most famed witch trial ever known. It claims to print a flawed old text by Mary's father.

Abraham Schweidler was pastor of Coserow, on the island of Usedom. In chapter seven, troops rob him and sack the church. His cow dies, food runs out, and troops burn half a nearby town. He flees with Mary and old Ilse to a cave in the woods. Starved children beg bread, and Mary shares what food is left. Want, war, and fear set the ground for the witch charge to come.
memorial-addresses-on-the-life-and-chara:
Memorial Addresses on William H. F. Lee were printed by Congress in 1892. The Government Printing Office in Washington made the book. Lee had served as a Representative from Virginia in Congress.

Speeches in the House and Senate make up the whole volume. Both chambers agreed in March 1892 to print eight thousand copies. Two thousand went to the Senate, and four thousand to the House. A portrait of Lee, engraved for the book, fronts the addresses. Fifty bound copies in morocco went to Lee's own family. The rest spread through both chambers for members and their state.
missionary-survey-as-an-aid-to-intellige:
Roland Allen and Thomas Cochrane published this study of mission planning in 1920. Allen, once an SPG missionary in North China, wrote the text. Cochrane, late principal of Union Medical College in Peking, studied the material with him. Their preface argues that missionary forces show little evidence of plan or method.

One region, they note, holds some 450 missionaries for three million people. Another, with twice the population, has only about twenty. Such gaps make survey, meaning systematic fact-finding, absolutely imperative. The book urges churches to distribute workers by knowledge rather than habit, so that cooperation in foreign missions becomes intelligent.
narrative-of-the-overland-expedition-of-:
Frederick J. Byerley compiled this tale from the Jardine brothers' journals. J. W. Buxton printed it in Brisbane in 1867. The brothers drove stock from Rockhampton to Cape York, in northern Queensland. Byerley worked as an engineer of roads in that district.

The book is inscribed to Sir Charles Nicholson of Sydney University. He is praised as an old, distinguished colonist. The Jardines crossed wild, unmapped country with cattle and horses. Rivers, hunger, and hostile encounters marked the long road north. Their trek opened Cape York to settlement, and this plain record, drawn from their own journals, keeps its grit.
nasa-tm-19660012971-extension-of-the-pho:
Norman F Ness at Goddard and John M Wilcox at the University of California, Berkeley, traced the Sun's surface magnetic field outward into space in this February 1965 paper. The photosphere is the Sun's visible surface, where the field is rooted. Magnetometer readings from the IMP-1 satellite measured the field near Earth. The authors compare those readings with observations of the Sun itself.

If the far field matches the surface pattern, the link between them can be mapped. Solar wind carries the field outward as it flows. Knowing that shape helps explain storms that reach Earth. Ness and Wilcox give an early, data-based picture of the field filling the space between Sun and Earth.
nasa-tm-19690000964-atlas-centaur-ac-12-:
Lewis Research Center evaluates the Atlas-Centaur AC-12 flight in this November 1968 memorandum. AC-12 launched on April 17, 1967, as the third operational Centaur flight. It carried Surveyor III toward the Moon on a lunar-intercept trajectory.

The ascent used parking-orbit mode. The Centaur first entered a circular orbit, then coasted under low-gravity conditions. From there it boosted the Surveyor spacecraft toward its lunar intercept path. Flight performance reports like this one check each vehicle system against predictions. They confirm the launch vehicle did its job for the lunar probe. Surveyor missions scouted the Moon ahead of crewed Apollo landings.
nasa-tm-19690003845-lighting-in-cryogeni:
Robert C. Hendricks and Kenneth J. Baumeister of Lewis Research Center show how to light fluids from inside in this report. Flow and heat-transfer studies often need illumination for visual observation and photography. The team submerged standard light bulbs in ordinary and cryogenic fluids to find safe operating conditions.

Successful operation happened whenever the bulb reached thermal equilibrium with its surroundings. A submerged bulb removes the need for a separate observation window. Windows bring leakage and lighting problems of their own. Internal bulbs can also provide localized heating along with light. A technical film supplement accompanied the report for readers who wanted motion pictures of the tests.
nasa-tm-19700024868-apollo-entry-summary:
James O. Rippey of the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston prepared this document on March 17, 1969. It is the Apollo entry summary for Mission F, flown with vehicle AS-505. Mission F was Apollo 10, the final rehearsal before the first landing attempt.

The summary gathers the entry information crews and planners needed in one place. Entry is the fiery return through Earth's air at the end of a mission. The document served flight planning, crew training, and the making of onboard data files. It stands as a final copy, kept as a library record at the Houston center.
nasa-tm-19720005939-a-method-for-star-ve:
S W Crigler of TRW Systems Group and T J Blucker of the Manned Spacecraft Center wrote this internal note on June 30, 1971. Blucker worked in the Mathematical Physics Branch in Houston. The note, MSC-04446, supports Project Apollo. It gives a method for turning telescope sightings into a star direction. Apollo navigators fixed their craft's attitude by sighting known stars.

The crew used the alignment optical telescope in the lunar module. Each sighting produced a spiral reading, a cursor reading, and a time. The method converts those three values into the measured star vector. The vector comes out in lunar module body coordinates. Guidance computers could then compare it with the expected star position.
nasa-tm-19720009626-determination-of-atm:
R. H. Lang and P. O. Minott wrote this NASA preprint in November 1971, numbered X-524-71-470, on measuring atmospheric turbulence with a single laser receiver. Turbulence bends and blurs light crossing the air, which limits telescope performance. The wave structure function is the measure that captures how strong that distortion is.

Earlier measurement schemes needed two optical systems and two detectors, gear many laboratories did not have. Lang and Minott describe and analyze a method using the single-beam laser receiver instead. The procedure masks the telescope aperture with an opaque screen pierced by two small holes. Covering one hole, then comparing the readings, lets the lone detector extract the structure function.
new-york-times-current-history-the-europ:
Volume one, number one of the New York Times Current History covers the European War from its start to March 1915. The Times Company published the monthly magazine in New York in 1915, with an index. Its first listed piece is by George Bernard Shaw.

Shaw's Common Sense About the War draws a storm of replies in the same number. Arnold Bennett calls it nonsense about Belgium, then states the German case. Cunninghame Graham picks at flaws in Shaw's logic, and Christabel Pankhurst calls him empty of good sense. Shaw also prints an open letter to President Wilson. The number shows a paper war fought beside the real one.
prairie-farmer-vol-56-no-1-january-5-188:
Chicago readers opened the new year with this issue of the Prairie Farmer, a weekly journal for the farm, orchard, and fireside. The paper was established in 1841 and now reached its fifty-sixth volume. The number is dated Saturday, January 5, 1884, priced at two dollars a year in advance. A transcriber's note warns that some original pages had corners torn off, with the missing text marked, a fitting scar for a paper that was read hard in farm kitchens.

Contents run the whole farm economy. Agriculture covers oat-grass and the barbed-wire business. Livestock pages give prices of 1883 and advice on docking horses. The dairy column teaches finance to creamery patrons. Other pages offer veterinary advice, garden news, poultry notes, and editorials. The editors take up the pork question in Europe and strong drink at home. One weekly issue preserves the information world of the 1884 corn belt.
sutherland-and-caithness-in-saga-time-or:
James Gray, of Oxford, wrote Sutherland and Caithness in Saga-Time, or The Jarls and the Freskyns, printed at Edinburgh by Oliver and Boyd in 1922. The book began as his presidential address to the Viking Society for Northern Research, then grew by amplification and revision.

Gray aims to interest the people of Sutherland and Caithness in their counties' early history. He aims at the three sagas above all. They bear on that history and on Orkney and Shetland too. Scottish records almost wholly fail for those times. Where records do survive he uses them. He gives special care to three hard questions. The first is the Caithness earldom succession after Earl John's death in 1231. The second is the first ancestors of the House of Sutherland. The third is the mystery of Lady Johanna of Strathnaver's descent.
the-california-birthday-book-prose-and-p:
The California Birthday Book holds prose and poetical selections from the writings of living California authors, with a brief life sketch of each. George Wharton James edited and arranged it, with an introduction, and the Arroyo Guild Press of Los Angeles put it out in 1909. James gave the book to his wife, his literary partner, whose judgment aided the selections.

An opening piece hails California as God's country: the land of golden thoughts, golden hills, golden mines, and golden deeds. In his introduction James says most selections refer to California herself. They cover her scenic glories, mountains, valleys, canyons, Yosemites, islands, and deserts. They cover her climate, flora and fauna, varied population, progress, and industries. Different authors tell it in prose and verse, so the book presents both California and California writers. An appendix gives further word on the authors and their work.
the-evolution-of-theology-an-anthropolog:
Thomas Henry Huxley's The Evolution of Theology, essay eight from Science and Hebrew Tradition, treats faith as a subject for the anthropologist. The rise, growth, decline, and fall of ideas about beings like men but lacking bodies, he says, fall under biology's care. With theology as a code of dogmas backed by threats, he wants no truck.

Nor does he treat it as a drug for life's pains. Huxley, Darwin's famed advocate, traces Hebrew faith from ghost lore to high monotheism. Field facts and frank prose mark his case, which still stirs debate.
the-golden-censer-or-the-duties-of-to-da:
John McGovern wrote The Golden Censer. Its subtitle is Or, The Duties of To-Day and the Hopes of the Future. McGovern was of the Chicago Tribune. The book sold by subscription only. It is dated 1884. A front picture of Time bears a line. The mill, it says, will never grind with the water that is past.

His preface states the aim of the book. It is to lighten the cares of today. It is to heighten the hopes of tomorrow. Each hope that is not a fool's beacon is built on the facts of today. Praise for a young person's talent rests on what that person does now. Hope, so grounded, makes a worker double his efforts. The book joins duty in the present to trust in what lies ahead.
the-lobster-fishery-of-maine-bulletin-of:
John N. Cobb, an agent of the United States Fish Commission, wrote The Lobster Fishery of Maine for the Commission's Bulletin, volume 19, pages 241 to 265, in 1899. Cobb reports that the steady decline of the New England lobster fishery had caused grave fears, above all in Maine, where the industry ranked first in importance. His paper gives the results of an investigation made in 1899, with statistics for the calendar year 1898 unless otherwise stated.

A section on the natural history of the lobster follows his thanks to dealers and fishermen. Cobb notes that little was known of the lobster's life and habits until recent years, and that this ignorance produced peculiar and sometimes useless state laws. Readers get both a fishery survey and an early plea for science-based rules.
the-nursery-volume-17-no-100-april-1875-: The Nursery reached its hundredth number in April 1875, in volume XVII of the Boston monthly for the youngest readers, published by John L. Shorey at $1.60 a year. Only the front matter and contents are present here, so the stories and poems themselves do not appear. The contents list The Boy Who Loved His Mother by Uncle Charles, Hunting for Easter-Eggs, About Flax, Barley, and Rye, Robert Southey's Cataract of Lodore, and Boiling Maple-Sugar.
the-outdoor-girls-at-the-hostess-house-o: Laura Lee Hope wrote The Outdoor Girls at the Hostess House, or Doing Their Best for the Soldiers, published in New York by Grosset and Dunlap. Only the title page and the publisher's series lists are present here, so the story itself does not appear. The Outdoor Girls list runs to nine volumes, ending with this one, after titles on Pine Island and in Army Service. Hope's Moving Picture Girls and Bobbsey Twins series fill the rest of the list.
the-von-toodleburgs-or-the-history-of-a-: F. Colburn Adams published The Von Toodleburgs, or the History of a Very Distinguished Family, at Philadelphia in 1868. Claxton, Remsen and Haffelfinger issued the volume, illustrated from original drawings by A. R. Waud. An illustration caption calls Hanz and Angeline Toodleburg the happiest couple in all the settlement. Only the title pages, Adams's list of earlier books, and the opening lines of a preface are present here. In those lines Adams doubts that prefaces serve any real usefulness.
the-youthful-wanderer-an-account-of-a-to:
Geo. H. Heffner wrote The Youthful Wanderer, dated 1876, for young Americans touring the Old World. Its tour crosses England, France, Belgium, Holland, and Germany. Switzerland, Italy, and Egypt complete the route. His preface recalls that learned ancients finished education by traveling. Europeans still keep that custom, he observes. Few Americans, separated by wide oceans, could afford the finishing course.

Steam power, Heffner argues, has changed the calculation. Ocean crossings once risked time, money, and health. Now the moment for American educational travel has come. His book adapts the grand tour to young readers' wants. It offers first glimpses of famous places through youthful eyes.
tom-swift-in-the-land-of-wonders-or-the-: Victor Appleton's Tom Swift in the Land of Wonders, the underground search for an idol of gold, is introduced by a numbered series list. Twenty-nine Tom Swift titles run from the motor-cycle through the big tunnel to this twentieth volume, then onward to the war tank, air scout, and undersea search. No chapter from the land of wonders itself follows the list. The series catalogue and title page are what is held in this record, so Appleton's underground adventure itself does not appear.
two-ghostly-mysteries-a-chapter-in-the-h:
J. S. Le Fanu's Two Ghostly Mysteries pairs A Chapter in the History of a Tyrone Family, first published in 1836, with The Murdered Cousin, from 1851. The first tale presents itself as an extract from the papers of Francis Purcell, a parish priest. Its narrator promises the very words of the woman who lived the story.

She was born Richardson, younger of two daughters of a Tyrone family of some distinction. Her sister, nearly six years older, married a Mr. Carew, a gentleman of property in the north. The teller's solemn air and deep religious principle, the introduction argues, rule out invention. Le Fanu frames the haunting as sworn testimony rather than fiction.
